The Petite Sirah blend, stainless fermentation followed by oak-treatment, and descriptors like chocolate-covered cherries and vanilla all point to a smooth, fruit-forward, commercial style with no named vineyard or producer story to lift it. Expect easy and soft with a short finish. What to look for: when the tasting notes are all dessert words (chocolate, vanilla, baking spice) and nothing savory or mineral, the wine is built to be smooth rather than interesting.

wines.name: Paul Direder Rosé Can 200ml Can
wines.verdict: Skip it. A 200ml canned rosé from an Austrian producer with no vintage, no grape variety named, and copy that leads with 'on the go' convenience — this is a format play, not a wine buy. The per-750ml equivalent of $14.96 is fine on paper, but there's nothing here to suggest farming intent, site specificity, or structure worth seeking out. What to look for: when buying canned wine, at minimum look for a named grape, a named producer with a real estate behind it, and ideally a vintage — those three details separate a convenience format from a throwaway product.

wines.name: Weingut Leo Hillinger Secco Rose 187ml
wines.verdict: Skip it. This is a carbonated Pinot Noir sparkling rosé in a 187ml mini — the listing explicitly says 'fermented in steel tanks and then carbonated,' which means no traditional-method character, no lees aging, no autolytic depth. It's fizzy pink wine in a small format, and at $28/750ml equivalent there are far better options. The Hillinger estate in Burgenland is a legitimate producer with real wines, but this Secco is a commercial convenience item. What to look for: for a sparkling rosé worth buying, look for 'traditional method' or 'méthode traditionnelle' on the label — that indicates the second fermentation happened in the bottle, which is what gives serious sparkling wine its texture and depth.

wines.name: Sean Minor California Series Sauvignon Blanc 2024 750ml
wines.verdict: Skip it. 'Vibrant and juicy' with grapefruit, citrus, and tropical fruit is the textbook commercial Sauvignon Blanc template — this is the industrial aromatic style the framework is specifically designed to flag. No sub-appellation, no soil reference, no vine age, no native yeast or barrel work, just a broad California label with selected-yeast aromatics. The critic scores (TP 92, WE 90) are consistent with the commercial style, not a structural read. What to look for: a genuinely interesting Sauvignon Blanc at any price will name a cool-climate sub-region (Loire Valley, Awatere Valley, Casablanca) or call out specific farming like native yeast fermentation or lees aging — tropical fruit aromatics are a red flag, not a selling point.

wines.name: J Dusi “Model M” Red Blend 2023
wines.verdict: Skip this one. At 14.9% ABV with tasting language centered on sweetness, richness, and confected fruit — "triple berry pie with bourbon whipped cream" — this reads as a wine built for immediate palatability rather than genuine structure or terroir expression. A four-variety Central Coast blend at $20 is rarely a farming story; this is a blending exercise. The Dusi family's old Zinfandel vines in Paso Robles are a genuinely historic asset, but this "Model M" blend at this price point appears to source broadly across the Central Coast rather than expressing that single-site heritage. The ABV and flavor profile together suggest the alcohol reads warm and the fruit reads confected rather than integrated. What to look for: if you want Dusi's genuine old-vine story, look for their single-varietal Zinfandel from the named Dusi Vineyard — that is the wine where their century-old vine heritage actually shows.  Dealbreakers: High ABV 14.9% with manipulated, confected tasting profile — 'triple berry pie with bourbon whipped cream' and 'lusciously rounded' language signals the style targets sweetness and viscosity over structural balance

wines.name: Wade Cellars Three by Wade California Cabernet Sauvignon 2022
wines.verdict: Skip it. This is a celebrity-branded, California-appellation Cabernet pitched at approachability, with 14.9% alcohol and copy built around generous fruit and easy drinking, which is the opposite of the site-driven bottles worth hunting. There is no named vineyard, soil, vine age or farming detail, so nothing here suggests more than a smooth, fruit-forward commercial wine. At this price, lots of bottles offer more structure and savory interest. What to look for: when the story leads with a famous name and 'approachable' rather than a place, you are paying for marketing.

wines.name: Los Noques Winemaker's Blend Limited Edition 2023 750ml
wines.verdict: Skip it. 'Winemaker's Blend Limited Edition' is lifestyle marketing language leading over any terroir story — there's no grape variety disclosed, no appellation, no named vineyard, and no producer credentials to anchor quality. At $14.99 the price is low, but the complete absence of identity makes this an unreliable buy. What to look for: when a label foregrounds the winemaker's name and 'limited edition' rather than a place or grape, that's a reliable signal that marketing is doing the work terroir should be doing.

wines.name: Alain De La Treille Le Rose 2025 750ml
wines.verdict: Skip it. This is a $15 Beaujolais-area rosé with a shop note that openly admits it's not complex, turns jammy with air, and finishes warm — not flattering signals. At this price the bar is low, but even so, there's nothing here to anchor a recommendation: no estate credential, no named terroir, no vine age, and the description points toward soft, simple commercial fruit rather than the kind of crisp, mineral Gamay-country rosé that punches above its weight. What to look for: at this price, hunt for a named Provence or Tavel estate, or a Loire rosé from a documented grower — those tend to have the saline, herb-driven precision this one lacks.

wines.name: Frenzy  'Mount Richmond Estate' Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc 2024/2025
wines.verdict: Skip it — this is exactly the commercial Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc style the savvy buyer routes around. The listing leads with guava, persimmon, peach, and melon — the full tropical-fruit template of high-yield Wairau blending. 'A carefully made blend of the best wines from selected vineyards' is multi-source procurement dressed up in nice language, not estate farming. Even at $18 there are sharper, more precise options. What to look for: look instead for a single-estate Sauvignon from a cooler sub-region like Awatere Valley or Martinborough, where the wines tend toward minerality and citrus pith rather than tropical sweetness.

wines.name: Gabriella Pinot Grigio Veneto 2024
wines.verdict: Skip it — generic Veneto Pinot Grigio at $11, and there's not much more to say. No producer identity, no vineyard, no soil detail, no vine age — just a broad Veneto appellation and boilerplate tasting notes that describe virtually every light Italian white on the market. It'll be clean, inoffensive, and forgettable. If you need a cheap, easy white for a crowd, it works, but the framework finds nothing here to recommend over a dozen better-value options in this price range. What to look for: Pinot Grigio worth buying carries at least a named sub-region (Friuli, Alto Adige) and ideally a single-estate name — those designations correlate strongly with actual flavor.

wines.name: Mokoroa Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc 2022 750ml
wines.verdict: Skip it. Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc without any sub-regional specificity, producer identity, or farming detail is the definition of a commodity wine — almost certainly multi-vineyard Wairau fruit processed for aromatic accessibility and quick sale. At $19 the price is low but not low enough to make it a value play over alternatives in the same range. No note is available to assess, which in this case is not a loss. What to look for: a Marlborough SB worth buying will name a specific sub-region (Awatere Valley, rather than just Marlborough), a single estate, or a winemaking departure like wild fermentation or barrel aging — without those signals, you are almost certainly getting the industrial template.

wines.name: Primore  Moscato Rosé 750ml
wines.verdict: Skip it — a sweet aromatic Moscato Rosé with no vintage, no producer credentials, and nothing here to justify even the modest $16 price beyond fruit-forward sweetness. The description leads entirely with 'sweet, aromatic, fruity with hints of flowers' and there is no terroir, no estate claim, no soil, no winemaker identity — this is the definition of a phantom commodity brand dressed in approachable packaging. Moscato is a legitimate category, but serious examples (Asti DOCG, single-estate Canelli) show up with traceable producers and minerality to balance the sweetness; nothing here suggests that. What to look for: when buying a sweet aromatic wine, a named appellation (like Asti or Moscato d'Asti DOCG) and a documented estate on the label are the minimum signals that someone cared about where the fruit came from.

wines.name: 2021 Orin Swift Papillon Red Blend
wines.verdict: Skip it. This is a brand-driven California red blend that leads with style over place, and nothing in the listing points to specific vineyards, old vines, or serious farming. Wines like this tend to be ripe, plush, and oak-influenced, aimed at a crowd-pleasing profile with little savory complexity or tension. At nearly $70 you are paying for the label, and the same money buys far more distinctive wine elsewhere. What to look for: a generic multi-sourced blend with no vineyard or sub-appellation named usually means you're paying for marketing, not terroir.

wines.name: Comte De Chamberi Bubbles
wines.verdict: Skip it unless you just want cheap, simple bubbles. A $10 sparkler from bulk-planted Airén in Castilla-La Mancha is a refreshment wine built for volume, and nothing in the listing points to a named site, serious producer, or documented lees aging. Expect light, clean, short-finishing fizz, likely made by the tank method. What to look for: if a sparkling wine doesn't say traditional method and give months or years on the lees, assume simple tank-fermented fizz and price it accordingly.

wines.name: Rubus Brut Blanc De Blancs 750ml
wines.verdict: Skip it. Rubus is an unidentified producer with no appellation, no lees-aging documentation, and no regional or geological anchor — the listing reads as a generic bulk sparkling wine dressed in minimalist branding. Blanc de Blancs in name only: without Champagne, Crémant, or Cava designation and no documented traditional-method tirage time, this almost certainly Charmat or tank-method, meaning no autolytic depth, no biscuit or toast character, just simple fresh fizz. At $12.99 the price is low, but even at this level you can find a Crémant d'Alsace or a Cava with documented traditional method and real lees contact for a few dollars more. What to look for: the words 'méthode traditionnelle' or a specific lees-aging duration on a sparkling wine label are your minimum signal that the fizz was made with the time-intensive process that creates real complexity.

wines.name: Quilt Fabric of the Land Red Blend 2024 750ml
wines.verdict: Skip this one. Quilt is a lifestyle-branded Napa-adjacent label — the name 'Fabric of the Land' and the 'deep plum with scarlet highlights' opener are textbook commercial wine copy — and it fires nearly every soft red flag in the book: multi-source California red blend, brand-forward positioning, and a description that emphasizes color and approachable fruit with no terroir, no producer story, and no structural ambition. At $35 the market is full of wines with actual farming credentials. What to look for: when a wine leads with its label design concept and color description rather than where and how the grapes were grown, that's a reliable sign the marketing budget outpaced the viticulture budget.

wines.name: Spy Valley Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc 2024
wines.verdict: Skip it — Spy Valley is the textbook example of the commercial Marlborough style this framework flags. 'Passionfruit and white nectarine' leading the note, 160 hectares of multi-variety production, and lifestyle-forward positioning ('impossible to ignore') all point in the wrong direction. The framework explicitly names Spy Valley as a commodity Marlborough bottling that doesn't benefit from any precision carve-out, and the description here confirms it. At $22, better options exist. What to look for: a family-owned Marlborough estate that isn't describing its wine as 'award-winning' and 'impossible to ignore' is likely more focused on the farming than the marketing.

wines.name: SLO Down Wines Sexual Chocolate Red 2022
wines.verdict: Skip it. The brand leads entirely with identity and storytelling — the listing offers no producer, no appellation beyond 'California,' no vineyard, no farming philosophy, and no specifics about the grapes beyond 'mostly Syrah blend.' 'Smooth finish' and 'ripe dark fruit' are exactly the descriptors that signal a wine made to a commercial flavor profile rather than a place. At $30 there are far more interesting options with actual terroir credentials. What to look for: at this price point, a California red should at least name an appellation and a farming approach — if the label leans harder on the name than on where the grapes grew, that's your cue to walk.  Dealbreakers: Lifestyle marketing leading over terroir; Phantom brand — sounds geographic, owns no specific dirt

wines.name: Highlands 41 Pinot Noir 2021 750ml
wines.verdict: Skip it. Paso Robles is a warm, high-yield region for Pinot Noir — the grape needs cool coastal influence (Sonoma Coast, Sta. Rita Hills, Willamette Valley, Burgundy) to show the transparency and tension that makes it worth drinking. A 2021 Paso Pinot at $18 from an unverified brand with generic fruit-and-spice copy has no structural case. What to look for: for Pinot Noir to be worth buying, the appellation matters more than almost any other grape — stick to regions where the climate actually suits the variety, and avoid warm inland designations regardless of price.

wines.name: Le Jade Viognier 2024 750ml
wines.verdict: Skip it. Viognier is at least an interesting indigenous southern Rhône variety, and Le Jade's version is from 2024 — fresh and likely aromatic — but again there is no producer identity, no estate, no soil claim, and the description (intense, seductive, ripe fruit) is pure aromatic-appeal marketing copy. Viognier without structural discipline becomes heavy and flabby quickly, and nothing here signals discipline. At $12 the value floor is low but the ceiling is also low. What to look for: a named Ardèche or Collines Rhodaniennes producer, or a Condrieu declassification, for Viognier that trades on site rather than just the grape's perfume.

wines.name: The Icon Rock Signature Sauvignon Blanc 2023 750ml
wines.verdict: Skip it. 'Very representative Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc' is almost a self-description of what the framework is built to avoid: high-yield Wairau Valley aromatic SB, and the note confirms it with 'freshness and vibrant fruit' plus what appears to be tropical fruit descriptors. The brand name — 'The Icon Rock Signature' — has no documented producer identity or estate behind it. At $20 there are better options in the Loire or even compliant New Zealand producers who farm for structure. What to look for: Marlborough SB worth buying will name a specific sub-region (Awatere Valley rather than just Marlborough), an estate, and describe the wine in terms of texture and mineral character rather than tropical fruit freshness.

wines.name: Sherwood Sauvignon Blanc 2025 750ml
wines.verdict: Skip it — identical wine to the six-bottle listing above, same score. The description is the classic high-yield Marlborough aromatic template (gooseberry, guava, lime) with no estate, soil, or structural credentials to distinguish it. At $17.99 the price is low, but there are better-structured whites at this price point from less-trodden regions. What to look for: if you want a sub-$20 Sauvignon Blanc with real tension, look for a Loire valley bottle (Muscadet is nearby in price and far more interesting structurally) or a Verdejo from Rueda — you'll get more substance for the same money.

wines.name: Odwyers Creek O'Dwyers Creek Sauvignon Blanc 2023 750ml
wines.verdict: Skip — O'Dwyers Creek is another multi-vineyard Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc with no vintage date visible, no producer pedigree, and a description that trails off before saying anything useful. The region is renowned for exactly the aromatic tropical style this framework doesn't reward, and at $27 you're paying a meaningful premium over the $17 commercial Marlborough options on this very shelf with no evidence of anything better behind it. No sub-regional specificity, no estate claim, no soil detail. What to look for: if you want a sub-$30 white with real mineral tension, the Quinta de Cabriz Dão on this shelf is a far more interesting buy — indigenous grapes, a specific Portuguese appellation, and a concrete grape blend.

wines.name: Hayes Ranch Pinot Noir 2022 750ml
wines.verdict: Skip it. Pinot Noir is one of the most terroir-sensitive and fraud-prone grapes in retail — at $14 with no stated appellation beyond implied California and a description leading with 'smooth and refined,' this is almost certainly a multi-vineyard Central Valley or blended-AVA pour with manufactured texture. The mushroom and clove note in the copy is a small positive signal, but not enough to overcome the anonymity. What to look for: Pinot Noir below $20 is almost always a compromise — if you're going to buy in this range, look for at least a named appellation (Willamette Valley, Sonoma Coast, Sta. Rita Hills) and a real producer name you can look up.

wines.name: Sherwood Sauvignon Blanc (6+ Bottles) 2025 750ml
wines.verdict: Skip it. The descriptor — gooseberry, guava, lime, fresh and zesty — is the exact commercial Marlborough aromatic template this framework is built to flag, and the 2025 vintage on a wine already on shelves suggests aggressive early release with no real development time. Sherwood is a large commercial Marlborough brand with no documented single-vineyard or precision-farming credential, and nothing in the listing points toward structure over aromatics. What to look for: if you want a sub-$20 Sauvignon Blanc with real tension, look for a Loire valley bottle (Muscadet is nearby in price and far more interesting structurally) or a Verdejo from Rueda — you'll get more substance for the same money.

wines.name: Fabbioli Cellars Raspberry Merlot 750ml
wines.verdict: Skip it. 'Raspberry Merlot' signals a fruit-forward novelty wine — the name and the description ('bright fresh raspberry juice upfront, jammy dark berries') suggest raspberry flavoring or co-fermentation rather than terroir-driven winemaking. There's no vintage date, no site information, and no farming philosophy on offer. Fabbioli Cellars is a small Virginia producer, which is a positive, but this particular bottling reads as a commercial sweetened novelty rather than a serious expression of the grape or the place. At $29 you can do significantly better. What to look for: when a wine's name leads with a fruit additive rather than a grape variety or place, that's a reliable signal to move on.  Dealbreakers: No vintage date — not a legitimate non-vintage blend; Lifestyle/novelty marketing leading over terroir (raspberry fruit addition implied by name and description)

wines.name: 689 Cellars Submission Red  2020 750ml
wines.verdict: Skip it. Submission Red is a textbook multi-region blend assembled for consistency and shelf appeal rather than any specific place — fruit sourced from five different AVAs is the opposite of a terroir-driven wine, and the marketing copy ('give into,' 'silky,' 'velvety') leads with lifestyle rather than farming. The 25% new French oak on a Zinfandel-Grenache-Malbec-Petite Sirah blend points toward a manipulated, fruit-forward style engineered for approachability, not structural interest. Critic scores from paid promotional panels don't override those structural signals. What to look for: when a wine's label names multiple distant growing regions in the same sentence, it's being blended for a flavor target, not expressing a place — seek out single-appellation or single-vineyard bottlings instead.  Dealbreakers: Phantom brand — multi-AVA sourcing across Sonoma, Napa, Lodi, Mendocino, and Paso Robles with no specific terroir; lifestyle marketing leads over terroir

wines.name: Los Noques Sauvignon Blanc 2024 750ml
wines.verdict: Skip this one. The description leads with tropical and citrus aromatics from a no-name Argentine producer at $14.99 — this is the commercial, high-yield Sauvignon Blanc template the framework is designed to flag. There's no estate identity, no named sub-region, no soil specificity, and no structural cues (native yeast, barrel work, cool-site minerality) that would suggest anything beyond a straightforward aromatic commodity bottling. At this price, better value exists elsewhere. What to look for: when a Sauvignon Blanc listing emphasizes tropical fruit aromas with no mention of site, soil, or winemaking method, it's almost always a refreshment-first commercial blend — look for 'estate,' a named sub-appellation, or 'flint/saline' language before committing.

wines.name: Orchard Lane Sauvignon Blanc 2024 750ml
wines.verdict: Skip it. This is a brand-forward, commercially styled New Zealand Sauvignon Blanc with no documented estate, no soil identity, and copy that leads entirely with fruit aromatics — exactly the industrial Marlborough style the framework is built to avoid. No origin specificity, no structure cues, no reason to choose this over a Loire Sauvignon at the same price. What to look for: when buying Sauvignon Blanc at this price, look for a named producer with a documented single estate or a Loire appellation (Muscadet, Menetou-Salon) on the label rather than a generic orchard-themed brand.  Dealbreakers: Phantom brand — no documented estate, no specific terroir, no regional identity

wines.name: Dansk Mjod Viking Blod 25 oz.
wines.verdict: Skip it. This is a hibiscus-infused mead — a honey-fermented drink, not grape wine — so the usual wine quality framework applies only loosely here. By mead standards, the listing offers very little to work with: no mention of honey variety or provenance, no indication of fermentation method or dryness, and the descriptor 'sweet, floral taste' suggests a straightforward commercial product aimed at novelty rather than complexity. The 19% ABV and sweet profile place it firmly in the dessert-drink category. At $33 for a 25oz bottle, the value isn't compelling for what it appears to be. What to look for: serious mead worth seeking out typically names the honey source (varietal or monofloral), emphasizes dryness or acid balance, and is made by a dedicated meadery with a documented fermentation process.

wines.name: Hayes Ranch Cabernet Sauvignon 2023 750ml
wines.verdict: Skip it. At $12 this is a mass-market California Cabernet with no stated origin beyond the implied Central Valley, no estate or farming credentials, and copy that leads with 'classic black cherry and cassis' — the hallmark of a commercial fruit-forward formula. No loopholes fire, no terroir is named, and the quality floor for anonymous sub-$15 California Cabernet is extremely low. What to look for: even at this price, a Cabernet worth buying names a specific appellation, states 'estate grown,' or comes from a documented producer with a reason to be in the bottle — price alone is not a reason.

wines.name: Kenwood Yulupa Chardonnay 750ml
wines.verdict: Skip it. Kenwood Yulupa is a multi-vineyard, no-vintage commercial Chardonnay from a large Sonoma negociant — the kind of wine where the winemaking (toast, vanilla, tropical sweetness) is doing the heavy lifting rather than any particular site or farming. The description reads as confected rather than terroir-driven: cream, sweet vanilla, tropical fruit are manipulated-oak markers, not vineyard character. At $14 there are far more honest bottles. What to look for: a named Chardonnay producer with a declared vintage and a specific appellation — even a modest one — so you know what you're actually buying.  Dealbreakers: No vintage date on a still wine — genuine non-vintage without declared blend rationale

wines.name: Le Jade Chardonnay 2023 750ml
wines.verdict: Skip it. Le Jade is a négociant southern French Chardonnay with no stated appellation, no soil story, and no producer identity beyond the brand. The description — yellow color, wonderful aromas — is generic retailer copy that tells you nothing about the wine. At $12 it may be drinkable, but there is no reason to choose it over a similarly priced bottle with an actual producer name attached. What to look for: even at this price, look for a named Languedoc or IGP producer rather than a brand label with no geographic specificity.

wines.name: Le Jade Sauvignon Blanc 2023 750ml
wines.verdict: Skip it. Le Jade Sauvignon Blanc is a southern French IGP brand wine with no named estate, no documented soil, and a descriptor — crisp, fragrant, aromatic — that matches the framework's red-flag language for industrial aromatic SB almost exactly. There is nothing here to suggest the wine is farmed for structure over easy aromatics. What to look for: a Loire Sauvignon Blanc (Menetou-Salon, Quincy, or a village Sancerre) for real mineral spine, or a single-estate Languedoc SB with documented native-yeast fermentation — both exist near this price point.

wines.name: Hayes Ranch Chardonnay 2025 750ml
wines.verdict: Skip it. "Vanilla and brown sugar aromatics" in a Chardonnay at $12 almost always signals heavy-handed oak treatment — either cheap stave-oak, chips, or a style engineered for softness rather than grown from a real site. There is no producer pedigree, no named vineyard, no regional specificity, and no farming philosophy on offer here — just a commodity label. What to look for: a Chardonnay worth buying at this price will name a specific appellation or producer philosophy, not lead with dessert aromatics.  Dealbreakers: Phantom brand — no specific terroir or estate identity evident; vanilla and brown sugar aromatics suggest heavy oak manipulation or flavoring rather than site-driven character

wines.name: Baku Wine Rose Semi Dry Wine
wines.verdict: Skip it — essentially no information exists to evaluate this wine. No vintage, no producer background, no grape variety, no region beyond the brand name, no ABV, and no tasting notes beyond 'semi dry rosé.' Semi-dry (off-dry) is not a disqualifier on its own, but a wine with this little provenance at any price cannot be recommended. What to look for: any rosé worth buying should at minimum name its grape variety, its origin, and ideally its producer — a label that leads only with a brand name and a sweetness descriptor is a signal to move on.  Dealbreakers: No vintage date; Phantom brand — no specific terroir, farming, or producer information available

wines.name: Kim Crawford Sauvignon Blanc 2025 375ml
wines.verdict: Skip it. Kim Crawford is the textbook example of industrial Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc — high-yield, multi-vineyard, selected-yeast, tropical-fruit-forward, and built for volume rather than site expression. Even at the per-bottle equivalent of $22, the framework is clear: this style offers no terroir specificity, no meaningful structure, and no reason to choose it over a Loire Sauvignon Blanc at a similar price. The 375ml format changes nothing about the wine inside. What to look for: for Sauvignon Blanc at this price, a Menetou-Salon or a Quincy from the Loire will give you real Kimmeridgian limestone character and a proper savory spine for a similar or lower spend.  Dealbreakers: Aromatic industrial Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc — multi-vineyard, selected-yeast, high-yield, no structural or terroir play

wines.name: "The Mascot" Exclusive Tasting
wines.verdict: Skip this entirely — it is not a wine you are buying. This listing is a $20 event ticket for an in-store tasting of The Mascot, with the fee credited toward any purchase made at the event. There is no bottle to evaluate here, and The Mascot itself is a Harlan Estate second label that, when sold as a bottle, carries a full Napa prestige premium with multi-site sourcing — good wine, but you are paying for the name and the family pedigree rather than irreplaceable terroir at a price that makes sense. What to look for: when a listing price seems surprisingly low for a famous name, check whether you are buying wine or buying access to wine.  Dealbreakers: Not a wine product — this is a ticketed tasting event, not a bottle of wine for purchase

wines.name: Lillet Rouge
wines.verdict: Skip it — Lillet Rouge is a fun aperitif mixer but not a serious wine buy at this price. It's an aromatized, fortified Bordeaux blend at 17% ABV, designed to be poured over ice with soda, not evaluated as a table wine. The flavor profile (grape soda, orange, vanilla) is the point, not a flaw, but there is nothing here in terms of terroir, farming, or structure that makes it a meaningful bottle purchase. What to look for: when buying aperitif-style bottles, look for producers who name their botanicals and base-wine source rather than leading with cocktail recipes.  Dealbreakers: Fortified/aromatized wine — evaluated as vermouth/aromatized category; BLIC+T machinery does not map literally to this product

wines.name: Kenwood Yulupa Cabernet Sauvignon 750ml
wines.verdict: No vintage date on a still Cabernet Sauvignon is an automatic red flag — it signals either a blended-year commercial product or a wine that someone didn't want you to ask about. Kenwood is a large commercial Sonoma brand (now owned by Jackson Family Wines) without estate farming or single-vineyard credibility, and the description's reliance on "plum reduction" and generic fruit descriptors confirms a polish-and-accessibility-first approach. Skip it. What to look for: a vintage date on a still red wine is the bare minimum of transparency — if it's not on the label, that's the producer telling you provenance doesn't matter to them, which usually means it shouldn't matter to you either.  Dealbreakers: No vintage date on a non-NV still wine

wines.name: Baku Wine  Tsinandali Dry White Wine
wines.verdict: Skip it. Tsinandali is a legitimate Georgian white appellation (Rkatsiteli and Mtsvane), but this bottle carries no vintage date and the producer Baku Wine has no documented estate identity or winemaking philosophy available — nothing here to evaluate meaningfully. What to look for: Georgian whites worth buying name a vintage and come from a documented estate or cooperative with a named winemaker.  Dealbreakers: No vintage date

wines.name: Geoffroy de Nouel L'Affreux Jojo 2021
wines.verdict: Skip this one entirely — there is simply not enough information to make a case for it. The listing gives no grape variety, no region, no producer track record, no ABV, and no meaningful description beyond the name 'L'Affreux Jojo' (which translates loosely as 'the dreadful rascal'). Without knowing the appellation, the variety, who made it, or what the wine tastes like, there is no rational basis for a purchase at any price. At $30 there are a dozen better-documented bottles on the same shelf. What to look for: any bottle worth $30 should show, at minimum, a named grape variety, a specific appellation, and a producer you can look up — if any of those three are missing from the label, walk away.  Dealbreakers: No vintage date — genuine non-vintage status unclear; listing provides no producer, region, grape variety, ABV, or appellation detail sufficient to evaluate

wines.name: Wine Club
wines.verdict: Not a wine product — this listing is a wine club membership subscription, not an individual bottle. There is no grape, no vintage, no terroir, and nothing to evaluate. Skip this entry entirely and look at the individual bottles the shop stocks instead. What to look for: when a listing has no vintage, no grape variety, and no appellation, it almost certainly isn't a bottle of wine.  Dealbreakers: Not a wine — this is a wine club subscription, not a bottle

wines.name: Sera Luce Sera Luce Venetian Spritz 4 pack 11 oz. Can
wines.verdict: Skip — this is a canned Venetian-spritz RTD (ready-to-drink), not a wine the framework can evaluate. It's an aromatized, flavored fizz product inspired by an Aperol-style spritz, sold in 11 oz cans. There's no terroir, no grape variety, no vintage, and no winemaking to assess. At roughly $5 per can it might be a fun poolside drink, but it has nothing to do with what this framework is built to find. What to look for: if you want the genuine Venetian spritz experience, buy a bottle of real Aperol or Campari and a bottle of Prosecco DOC from a named producer — you'll get far more for the money and actual wine in the glass.  Dealbreakers: Out of scope — aromatized/spritz RTD product, not a still or traditional-method wine; BLIC+T and loophole framework does not apply

wines.name: Staff Pick Six
wines.verdict: Not a wine — a staff-curated gift bundle. There are no grapes, no vintage, no terroir, no winemaker, and no fixed bottle to evaluate here. The quality, value, and character of this package depend entirely on what the shop puts in it on the day of purchase, which cannot be assessed in advance. If you want to use this framework to make a buying decision, pick individual bottles instead.

wines.name: Staff Pick Mixed Case of Wine
wines.verdict: Not a wine — a staff-curated twelve-bottle bundle. Same issue as the six-bottle version: no fixed contents, no terroir, no producer, nothing to evaluate. The 10% discount is a reasonable deal if you trust the shop's palate, but that is a relationship call, not a wine-quality call. Buy individual bottles if you want a reasoned recommendation.

wines.name: Wine Camp *Session 1*
wines.verdict: Skip this listing entirely — it's a ticketed wine education event (Wine Camp, July 14th at Arrowine), not a bottle of wine. There's nothing to evaluate here in terms of quality or value. What to look for: when a listing is a class or tasting event rather than a product, no wine scoring applies — check the shop's event calendar separately.  Dealbreakers: Not a wine product — this is a ticketed tasting event and is out of scope for wine evaluation

wines.name: Weingut Steininger STEININGER  VERJUS ALCOHOL FRRE ZWEIGELT ROSE  NV 750ml
wines.verdict: This is a non-alcoholic verjus product, not a fermented wine — the listing explicitly describes it as 'alcohol free' and the producer's own note calls it a 'non-alcoholic recommendation.' The value and quality framework here is built for fermented beverages, so a score in either direction would be meaningless. What to look for: if you want a low-intervention sparkling alternative, look for a lightly sparkling, low-ABV pét-nat (pétillant naturel) rather than a de-alcoholized product — the fermentation is real and the character follows.  Dealbreakers: Non-alcoholic/de-alcoholized product — out of scope for this framework

wines.name: Raspberry Preserves 7.4 oz  - Maison Perrotte
wines.verdict: This is raspberry jam, not wine — the evaluation framework simply doesn't apply here. What to look for: when browsing a wine shop's online catalogue, filter by ABV or category to avoid non-wine products slipping into the queue.  Dealbreakers: Not a wine — this is a food product (fruit preserves). Out of scope for this evaluation framework.

wines.name: SEA GLASS CHRISTMAS TREE CLASS & WINE TASTING DEC 6TH 2PM 750ml
wines.verdict: Skip — this is not a wine. The listing is an event ticket for a Christmas tree decorating class with a wine tasting on December 6th, priced at $89.95. There is nothing to evaluate here under any wine quality framework. What to look for: when browsing a shop's online catalogue, filter out event listings by checking that the product has a producer, a region, and a vintage before spending time on evaluation.  Dealbreakers: Not a wine product — this is a ticketed event listing (Christmas tree class and wine tasting), not a bottle of wine available for purchase evaluation

wines.name: GNOME PAINTING & WINE TASTING OCTOBER 4,  2-4 PM 750ml
wines.verdict: This is not a wine listing — it appears to be a shop event booking (Gnome Painting & Wine Tasting, October 4, 2–4 PM) that has been scraped into the product catalogue by mistake. There is no wine to evaluate here. What to look for: if you are looking for the wine served at this event, ask the shop directly — it won't be on the shelf under this listing.  Dealbreakers: No vintage date; Phantom brand — not a wine product

wines.name: Herpac Bluefin Tuna Ventresca Smoked Carpaccio
wines.verdict: Not a wine. This is a tinned or packaged smoked bluefin tuna belly — a food product that has ended up in the wine catalogue by mistake. There is nothing to evaluate here against any wine quality criteria. What to look for: if you're pairing something with this, a dry fino Sherry or a crisp Muscadet would be the classic match for oily, briny fish.  Dealbreakers: Not a wine — this is a smoked tuna food product (Herpac Bluefin Ventresca Smoked Carpaccio) and is outside the scope of wine evaluation entirely

wines.name: Tuffy Stone Original BBQ Sauce
wines.verdict: Not a wine. This is a bottled barbecue sauce from pitmaster Tuffy Stone — a food condiment, not a fermented beverage. There's nothing to score here against a wine framework. What to look for: if it's on the shelf next to the wine, someone mis-tagged it; look elsewhere in the shop for your bottle.  Dealbreakers: Not a wine — BBQ sauce is a non-fermented condiment product; out of scope for wine evaluation

wines.name: MATCHES -  CHAMPAGNE SHACK SQUARE BOX N/A
wines.verdict: Skip — this listing is a box or packaging accessory ('Champagne Shack Square Box'), not a bottle of wine. There is nothing to evaluate here on any wine quality dimension. What to look for: make sure the listing you're buying is an actual bottle of wine, not gift packaging or an accessory.  Dealbreakers: No vintage date — non-vintage status unverified; listing appears to be a non-wine accessory or packaging item (Champagne Shack square box), not an evaluable wine
